en: I am free after three if you want to discuss.
tamil: நீங்க பேசணும்னா மூணு மணிக்கு மேல நான் ஃப்ரீ.
context: Offering a time to a colleague for a talk.
explain: 'If you want to' makes the offer flexible and polite.
usage: Use it with a teammate who needs a talk with you during a busy day.
leelaQ: When are you free to talk in the day?
answer: I am usually free in the afternoon after lunch.

en: I'm going to talk to my manager about the deadline.
tamil: டெட்லைனைப் பத்தி என் மேனேஜர்கிட்ட பேசப் போறேன்.
context: Saying what you plan to do about a tight deadline.
explain: 'Going to' shows a plan you have already decided to follow.
usage: Use it with a teammate when you have a plan to raise a problem with your boss.
leelaQ: Who will you talk to if a deadline is too tight?
answer: I am going to talk to my manager and ask for more time.

en: Should I add you to this email?
context: Checking if a colleague should be in the mail loop.
explain: 'Should I' asks for advice or permission about your own action.
usage: Use it at work when you are not sure who should receive a message.
leelaQ: Who do you add in your office emails?
answer: I add my manager and the team members who need to know.

en: Is the client joining the call?
context: Asking before a meeting begins.
explain: 'Is joining' can talk about a plan for the near future.
usage: Use it just before an online meeting when you are not sure who will attend.
leelaQ: Who usually joins your online meetings?
answer: Our team members and sometimes the client join them.

en: Our manager is travelling, so the meeting is online.
tamil: எங்க மேனேஜர் பயணத்துல இருக்காரு, அதனால மீட்டிங் ஆன்லைன்ல.
context: Explaining why the meeting is not in the office.
explain: 'So' joins a reason with a result.
usage: Use it when a teammate asks why the meeting is held online.
leelaQ: Do you prefer online or office meetings?
answer: I prefer office meetings because it is easy to talk face to face.

en: My colleague covered for me when I was sick.
tamil: நான் உடம்பு சரியில்லாம இருந்தப்போ என் கொலீக் என் வேலையை பாத்துக்கிட்டாரு.
context: Thanking a teammate who helped you.
explain: 'Covered for me' means did my work while I was away.
usage: Use it to thank a colleague or to tell a manager how teammates support each other.
leelaQ: Who helps you at work when you are away?
answer: My teammate takes care of my tasks when I am on leave.

en: We have not received the client's reply yet.
context: Updating a manager on a pending reply.
explain: 'Have not ... yet' means something is still pending.
usage: Use it when your manager asks if the client has answered.
leelaQ: What do you do when a client does not reply?
answer: I send a reminder and then I call them.

en: Has everyone received the agenda?
context: Checking before a meeting starts.
explain: 'Has everyone' takes a singular verb. An agenda is a list of topics for a meeting.
usage: Use it as an organiser before a meeting to make sure people are ready.
leelaQ: What does a good meeting agenda have?
answer: It has the topics, the time and the names of the speakers.

en: I wrote down all the points from the meeting.
tamil: மீட்டிங்ல இருந்த எல்லா பாயின்ட்களையும் எழுதி வச்சிருக்கேன்.
context: Telling a colleague you have the meeting notes.
explain: 'Wrote down' is the past of 'write down'. It means to make a written note.
usage: Use it when a teammate missed the meeting and wants the details.
leelaQ: Do you take notes in meetings?
answer: Yes, I write the main points in my notebook.

en: You should share your ideas in the meeting.
context: Encouraging a shy teammate to speak up.
explain: 'Should' is used to give friendly advice.
usage: Use it to encourage a junior colleague who stays quiet in meetings.
leelaQ: Do you share your ideas in meetings?
answer: Yes, I share my ideas when I feel confident about them.

en: Your feedback helped me a lot.
tamil: உங்க ஃபீட்பேக் எனக்கு ரொம்ப உதவியா இருந்துச்சு.
context: Thanking a senior for useful comments.
explain: 'Helped me a lot' is a warm way to thank someone for advice.
usage: Use it after a manager or senior gives you good feedback on your work.
leelaQ: Who gave you useful feedback recently?
answer: My team lead gave me good feedback on my last report.

en: We are going to launch the update next week.
tamil: நாங்க அடுத்த வாரம் அப்டேட்டை வெளியிடப் போறோம்.
context: Announcing a plan to the whole team.
explain: 'Going to' is good for planned events. 'Launch' means to start something new.
usage: Use it when you tell the team or a client about a planned release.
leelaQ: What is your team planning for next week?
answer: We are going to test the new feature and share it.

en: We have a new target for this month.
tamil: இந்த மாசத்துக்கு எங்களுக்கு ஒரு புது டார்கெட் இருக்கு.
context: Telling the team about a new goal.
explain: 'Have' is used here for something that belongs to the team.
usage: Use it when a manager shares monthly goals with the team.
leelaQ: What target do you have this month?
answer: I have to finish three tasks before the end of the month.

en: I could finish early because the team helped.
tamil: டீம் உதவுனதால நான் சீக்கிரம் முடிக்க முடிஞ்சது.
context: Crediting your teammates for a quick finish.
explain: 'Could' is used here for ability in the past. 'Because' gives the reason.
usage: Use it to give credit to your team when your manager praises you.
leelaQ: How does teamwork help you at work?
answer: It helps me finish my tasks faster and learn new things.

en: Our team lead sends the daily summary at six.
tamil: எங்க டீம் லீட் தினமும் ஆறு மணிக்கு சுருக்கத்தை அனுப்புவாரு.
context: Explaining the daily routine to a new joiner.
explain: The simple present is used for fixed daily routines. 'Sends' takes an 's' after 'lead'.
usage: Use it to explain office routines to a new person in your team.
leelaQ: What daily reports do you send or receive?
answer: I get a daily summary from my team lead in the evening.

en: I have attached the document to this email.
context: Writing the first lines of an email with a file.
explain: 'Have attached' is the usual phrase in emails. It tells the reader to check the file.
usage: Use it in an email when you send a file along with your message.
leelaQ: What do you write when you send a file by email?
answer: I write that I have attached the file and ask them to check it.

en: He explained the problem very clearly.
context: Praising a colleague after a meeting.
explain: 'Clearly' is an adverb that tells how he explained.
usage: Use it to praise a teammate in front of others or to your manager.
leelaQ: Can you explain your work clearly to others?
answer: Yes, I use simple words and give small examples.

en: Could you explain that point again?
tamil: அந்த பாயின்ட்டை ஒருமுறை திரும்ப விளக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a speaker to repeat politely.
explain: 'Could you' sounds more polite than 'can you'.
usage: Use it in a meeting or a call when you missed a detail.
leelaQ: How do you ask someone to repeat something?
answer: I say could you explain that again, please.

en: The meeting has been moved to four o'clock.
context: Telling a colleague about a new meeting time.
explain: 'Has been moved' shows a change that is already done. It is common in office updates.
usage: Use it when you tell your team that a meeting time has changed.
leelaQ: What do you say when a meeting time changes?
answer: I tell my team that the meeting has been moved to a new time.

en: We have finished almost sixty percent of the work.
context: Giving a progress update to a manager.
explain: 'Almost' means nearly. 'Have finished' links the work done to the present.
usage: Use it when your manager asks how much work is complete.
leelaQ: How much of your work is finished today?
answer: I have finished about half of my tasks.

en: I agree with you, but I have one small concern.
tamil: நீங்க சொல்றது சரிதான், ஆனா எனக்கு ஒரு சின்ன கவலை இருக்கு.
context: Politely raising a doubt in a discussion.
explain: Start with 'I agree' and then use 'but' to add your doubt. It sounds polite.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you accept an idea but want to raise a point.
leelaQ: How do you raise a doubt politely in a meeting?
answer: I say I agree first, and then I explain my small concern.

en: Did the manager approve my leave?
context: Asking a teammate or HR about leave status.
explain: 'Approve' means to officially say yes to something.
usage: Use it with HR or a colleague when you are waiting for leave approval.
leelaQ: When do you apply for leave in your company?
answer: I apply at least a week before I need the leave.

en: The feedback was honest, and I accepted it.
tamil: ஃபீட்பேக் நேர்மையா இருந்துச்சு, நானும் அதை ஏத்துக்கிட்டேன்.
context: Telling a friend how you took criticism.
explain: 'And' joins two past actions. 'Accepted' means took it without anger.
usage: Use it to show a mature attitude when you talk about criticism.
leelaQ: How do you feel when you get feedback?
answer: I feel a little nervous, but I try to learn from it.

en: I will send you the updated file by evening.
context: Promising a colleague a revised document.
explain: 'Will' is used for a promise. 'By evening' sets a clear deadline.
usage: Use it with a teammate who is waiting for your work.
leelaQ: When do you usually send your reports to your manager?
answer: I usually send them before lunch so my manager can check them.

en: What time is the review call?
context: Asking a teammate about a meeting time.
explain: A short and common question for schedules.
usage: Use it with a colleague when you forgot the time of a meeting.
leelaQ: What time does your office day start?
answer: It starts at nine thirty in the morning.

en: We must finish this work before Friday.
context: Reminding the team about a firm deadline.
explain: 'Must' shows something very important or necessary.
usage: Use it when a deadline is fixed and the whole team needs to hurry.
leelaQ: What must you finish this week?
answer: I must finish my pending tasks and send them to my manager.

en: Good work, everyone, we reached our target.
context: Thanking the team after a successful month.
explain: 'Reached our target' is a common phrase for completing a goal.
usage: Use it as a manager or senior to thank the team after a success.
leelaQ: How do you celebrate with your team?
answer: We usually have tea together and share some sweets.

en: Which task should I do first?
context: Asking a manager how to set priorities.
explain: 'Which' is used when there are a few known choices.
usage: Use it with a manager when you have many pending tasks.
leelaQ: How do you decide which task to do first?
answer: I do the urgent and important task first.

en: I have already sent you two reminders.
context: Politely telling someone you waited for a reply.
explain: 'Already' shows that it happened before now and a bit more than expected.
usage: Use it politely with a colleague who has not replied to your emails.
leelaQ: What do you do if someone does not reply to your email?
answer: I send a polite reminder and then I call them.

en: Can you please join the call on time?
tamil: தயவுசெஞ்சு சரியான நேரத்துக்கு காலுக்கு வர முடியுமா?
context: Asking a teammate to be punctual.
explain: 'Please' in the middle makes it a gentle request.
usage: Use it as a team lead when people join meetings late.
leelaQ: Why is it important to be on time?
answer: It shows respect and saves everyone's time.

en: Please do not share this file outside the team.
context: Giving a warning about a confidential file.
explain: 'Please do not' is a polite and firm order.
usage: Use it when you send private office documents to your colleagues.
leelaQ: What office files should you keep private?
answer: Salary details and client data should stay private.

en: Can we start the meeting now?
context: Asking in a meeting room when everyone is ready.
explain: 'Can we' is a friendly way to suggest an action together.
usage: Use it as an organiser when you see all people have arrived.
leelaQ: How do you start a meeting?
answer: I greet everyone and say what we will discuss today.

en: Can you give me some feedback on my work?
tamil: என் வேலைக்கு கொஞ்சம் ஃபீட்பேக் கொடுக்க முடியுமா?
context: Asking a senior to review your work.
explain: 'Some feedback' is correct. 'Feedbacks' is not used in standard English.
usage: Use it with a senior when you want to improve your work.
leelaQ: Who do you ask for feedback?
answer: I ask my team lead because he knows my work well.

en: The design team is waiting for our approval.
tamil: டிசைன் டீம் நம்ம ஒப்புதலுக்காக காத்துக்கிட்டு இருக்காங்க.
context: Reminding your manager about a pending approval.
explain: 'Is waiting for' needs 'for' before the thing you wait for.
usage: Use it when work is stopped because someone has not approved it yet.
leelaQ: What is the last thing you waited for at work?
answer: I waited for my manager's approval on a leave request.

en: When will the report be ready?
context: Asking a colleague about the time of a report.
explain: 'When will' asks about a future time.
usage: Use it when you are waiting for a document from a teammate.
leelaQ: When do you expect your next big task to finish?
answer: I expect to finish it by the end of next week.

en: Our boss appreciated the team's effort.
context: Telling your family about a good day at work.
explain: 'Appreciated' is a stronger word than 'liked'. It shows respect for hard work.
usage: Use it with friends or family when you share how the boss reacted.
leelaQ: Does your boss appreciate your work?
answer: Yes, he often says thank you after a project.

en: Please mute your mic when you are not speaking.
tamil: பேசாத நேரத்துல உங்க மைக்கை மியூட் பண்ணுங்க.
context: Reminding people in an online meeting.
explain: 'Mute' means to turn off the sound. 'When' joins the request to the condition.
usage: Use it as a host in an online meeting when there is background noise.
leelaQ: Why should you mute your mic in a call?
answer: Because the background noise disturbs the speaker.

en: I'll make the changes and send it again.
context: Replying to a reviewer after getting comments.
explain: 'I'll' is the short form of 'I will'. It is natural in spoken English.
usage: Use it when your manager or client gives you comments on your work.
leelaQ: What do you do after you get comments on your work?
answer: I read them carefully, make the changes and send it again.

en: The team worked late to meet the deadline.
tamil: டெட்லைனை எட்டுறதுக்கு டீம் லேட்டா வரைக்கும் வேலை பண்ணுச்சு.
context: Telling a friend how hard the team worked.
explain: 'To meet the deadline' means to finish the work on time.
usage: Use it when you describe a busy week to friends or to your manager.
leelaQ: Have you ever worked late for a deadline?
answer: Yes, I worked until nine o'clock to finish a report.

en: Everyone in our team helps each other.
tamil: எங்க டீம்ல எல்லாரும் ஒருத்தருக்கொருத்தர் உதவி பண்ணுவாங்க.
context: Describing your team spirit in an interview or chat.
explain: 'Each other' is used when two or more people do the same thing to one another.
usage: Use it in an interview or with a friend when you talk about your team.
leelaQ: How is the teamwork in your office?
answer: Our teamwork is good, and everyone helps when someone is busy.

en: I completed the testing yesterday.
context: Giving a status update to your team lead.
explain: 'Completed' is past tense. 'Yesterday' tells us the work was finished before today.
usage: Use it in a daily update when you report work you have already finished.
leelaQ: What work did you finish yesterday?
answer: I finished the testing and wrote a short report yesterday.

en: What is the deadline for this task?
context: Asking your manager about the last date.
explain: 'What is the ... for' is a clear question for details.
usage: Use it when you get a new task and need to know the due date.
leelaQ: What do you ask when you get a new task?
answer: I ask the deadline and who will check the work.

en: I did not understand the last point.
context: Asking politely for clarity in a meeting.
explain: 'Did not' with the base verb makes a past negative.
usage: Use it in a meeting before you ask the speaker to explain again.
leelaQ: What do you do when you do not understand something?
answer: I ask the person to explain it once more.

en: The report is not ready yet.
context: Replying to a manager who asks for the report.
explain: 'Not ready yet' means it will be ready later.
usage: Use it when a manager asks for something before you have finished.
leelaQ: What do you say when your work is not ready?
answer: I say it is not ready yet and tell them when it will be.

en: I will update the status sheet after lunch.
tamil: மதிய சாப்பாட்டுக்கு அப்புறம் ஸ்டேட்டஸ் ஷீட்டை அப்டேட் பண்றேன்.
context: Telling a teammate when you will fill the tracker.
explain: 'After lunch' is a simple time phrase for a plan.
usage: Use it with a team lead who asks for an updated tracker.
leelaQ: What do you do after lunch at work?
answer: I answer my emails and continue with my tasks.

en: Kindly reply to this mail as soon as possible.
tamil: இந்த மெயிலுக்கு முடிஞ்சவரைக்கும் சீக்கிரம் பதில் சொல்லுங்க.
context: Writing a formal email to a client.
explain: 'Kindly' is common in Indian official English. 'As soon as possible' means quickly.
usage: Use it in an email when you need a fast answer from someone.
leelaQ: How do you ask for a quick reply in an email?
answer: I write please reply as soon as possible, and I say thank you.

en: I think we should try a different approach.
tamil: நாம வேற மாதிரி முயற்சி பண்ணலாம்னு நினைக்கிறேன்.
context: Suggesting a new way to solve a problem.
explain: 'I think we should' is a soft way to give a suggestion.
usage: Use it in a team discussion when the current plan is not working.
leelaQ: How do you suggest a new idea to your team?
answer: I say I think we should try a different way.

en: I was in a client call when you messaged.
tamil: நீங்க மெசேஜ் பண்ணப்போ நான் கிளையன்ட் காலுல இருந்தேன்.
context: Explaining why you replied late.
explain: 'Was' with 'when' shows what you were doing at that time.
usage: Use it when a colleague asks why you did not reply on time.
leelaQ: Why do people reply late to messages?
answer: Maybe they are in a meeting or busy with another task.

en: Someone has to talk to the client today.
context: Pushing the team to take responsibility.
explain: 'Has to' shows that something is necessary. 'Someone' takes a singular verb.
usage: Use it in a team chat when a task needs an owner.
leelaQ: Who talks to the client in your team?
answer: Our team lead talks to the client most of the time.

en: I will check with the team and get back to you.
context: Replying to a client when you do not know the answer yet.
explain: 'Get back to you' means to reply later with the answer. It is very common at work.
usage: Use it with a client or manager when you need time to find the answer.
leelaQ: What do you say when you do not know the answer?
answer: I say I will check and get back to them soon.

en: Did you read my email?
context: Checking if a colleague saw your mail.
explain: 'Did' starts a past question, and the main verb stays in the base form.
usage: Use it politely with a teammate who has not responded to your mail.
leelaQ: How often do you check your emails?
answer: I check them in the morning, after lunch and in the evening.

en: Kindly review the document and share your comments.
context: Asking a colleague to check a document.
explain: Two actions joined with 'and'. 'Review' means to check carefully.
usage: Use it in an email when you want someone to check your document.
leelaQ: What do you do before you send a document?
answer: I read it twice and ask a friend to check it.

en: I am sharing my screen now.
tamil: நான் இப்போ என் ஸ்கிரீனை ஷேர் பண்றேன்.
context: Starting a screen share in an online meeting.
explain: 'Am sharing' tells what you are doing at this moment.
usage: Use it in an online meeting before you show a presentation or file.
leelaQ: Do you attend online meetings?
answer: Yes, I attend two or three online meetings every week.

en: How is the work going?
context: Checking on a colleague's progress in a friendly way.
explain: 'How is ... going' is a casual way to ask for an update.
usage: Use it as a friendly check-in with a teammate or junior.
leelaQ: How is your work going these days?
answer: It is going well, but I am a bit busy.

en: I can take this task if nobody is free.
tamil: யாரும் ஃப்ரீயா இல்லன்னா இந்த வேலையை நான் எடுத்துக்குறேன்.
context: Offering to help the team with extra work.
explain: 'Can' shows that you are ready and able. 'If' gives the condition.
usage: Use it when your team is short of people and you want to help.
leelaQ: When do you offer to help your teammates?
answer: I offer help when they have too much work.

en: Can we move the review to Thursday afternoon?
context: Asking to change the time of a review.
explain: 'Can we move' is a friendly way to ask for a new time.
usage: Use it when you have another urgent task on the planned day.
leelaQ: What do you do if you cannot attend a review on time?
answer: I tell my manager early and ask for another time.

en: What is your opinion on this plan?
tamil: இந்த பிளானைப் பத்தி உங்க கருத்து என்ன?
context: Asking a teammate to share a view in a discussion.
explain: 'Opinion' means what you personally think about something.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you want everyone to share their views.
leelaQ: Do you like to share your ideas in team meetings?
answer: Yes, I share my ideas, but I listen to others first.

en: I have worked with this client for two years.
tamil: நான் இந்த கிளையன்ட்டோட ரெண்டு வருஷமா வேலை பண்றேன்.
context: Saying how long you know the client.
explain: 'For two years' with 'have worked' means it started in the past and is still going.
usage: Use it in an interview or meeting to show your experience.
leelaQ: How long have you worked in your company?
answer: I have worked here for three years.

en: Please find the details in the attached file.
context: Writing a formal email with an attachment.
explain: 'Please find' is a common formal phrase in business emails.
usage: Use it in a formal email when you send details as an attachment.
leelaQ: How do you start an email with details?
answer: I write a short greeting and then I mention the attached file.

en: I respectfully disagree with that point.
context: Disagreeing politely with a senior in a meeting.
explain: 'Respectfully' makes a disagreement sound polite and professional.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you do not accept someone's idea but want to be polite.
leelaQ: How do you disagree with someone at work?
answer: I stay calm and say I respectfully disagree, and then I give my reason.

en: We have a team lunch on Friday.
context: Inviting a new colleague to join the group.
explain: The simple present can talk about fixed future events like a plan.
usage: Use it to inform or invite a colleague about a group event.
leelaQ: Does your team go out for lunch together?
answer: Yes, we go out once a month to a nearby restaurant.

en: I have already informed the whole team.
context: Telling your manager the team knows about the change.
explain: 'Have informed' with 'already' shows the work is done before now.
usage: Use it when your manager asks if everyone knows about an announcement.
leelaQ: How do you tell your team about a change?
answer: I send a short message to the group and also tell them in person.

en: I will join the call in five minutes.
context: Messaging the team when you are a little late.
explain: 'In five minutes' means five minutes from now.
usage: Use it in a chat when you are not able to join an online call on time.
leelaQ: What do you say if you are late for a call?
answer: I say I will join in a few minutes and say sorry.

en: Did we miss anything important?
context: Checking at the end of a meeting.
explain: A good closing question. It shows that you care about the details.
usage: Use it at the end of a meeting or when you check a list before sending.
leelaQ: What do you check before you end a meeting?
answer: I check the action points and who will do them.

en: Are you facing any problem with this task?
tamil: இந்த வேலையில உங்களுக்கு ஏதாவது பிரச்சனை இருக்கா?
context: Asking a junior colleague if they need help.
explain: 'Facing a problem' is a common phrase in Indian English for 'having a problem'.
usage: Use it as a senior when a teammate looks stuck.
leelaQ: What problem did you face at work recently?
answer: I could not find a file, and my colleague helped me.

en: Who will write the minutes of this meeting?
context: Asking at the start of a team meeting.
explain: 'Minutes' are the written record of a meeting.
usage: Use it at the start of a meeting so that someone takes the responsibility.
leelaQ: Do you ever write the minutes for your team?
answer: Yes, I write them sometimes when my turn comes.

en: Don't blame anyone, just fix the issue.
tamil: யாரையும் குத்தம் சொல்லாதீங்க, பிரச்சனையை சரி பண்ணுங்க.
context: Calming a team during a work problem.
explain: 'Don't' plus a verb is a negative order. The second part gives the right action.
usage: Use it as a team lead when people are arguing about whose mistake it was.
leelaQ: Why is it better to solve a problem than blame someone?
answer: Because blaming wastes time and the problem remains.

en: Will you be at the team meeting tomorrow?
context: Checking a colleague's presence.
explain: 'Will you be at' asks about presence at a future event.
usage: Use it when you plan a discussion and need someone to attend.
leelaQ: Will you attend any meeting tomorrow?
answer: Yes, I have a review meeting at eleven.

en: Where did you save the final file?
context: Looking for a document in a shared folder.
explain: 'Where did you' asks about a place in the past. 'Save' stays in the base form.
usage: Use it when a teammate shares a file and you cannot find it.
leelaQ: Where do you keep your office files?
answer: I keep them in a shared folder and also on my laptop.

en: Can you help me with this report?
context: Asking a senior colleague for help.
explain: 'Help me with' is followed by the task.
usage: Use it with a senior colleague when you are stuck on your work.
leelaQ: Who do you ask for help at work?
answer: I ask my senior colleague because he is kind and knows a lot.

en: I will send the report by tomorrow evening.
context: Promising a manager when the report will come.
explain: 'Will' makes a promise. 'By' gives the last time for the work.
usage: Use it with a manager or client when you promise a time for your work.
leelaQ: When will you send your next report?
answer: I will send my next report by Friday afternoon.

en: She is preparing the presentation for the review.
tamil: அவங்க ரிவியூக்கான பிரசன்டேஷனை தயார் பண்ணிட்டு இருக்காங்க.
context: Explaining where a colleague is right now.
explain: 'Is preparing' shows work in progress.
usage: Use it when someone asks about a colleague who is busy with a task.
leelaQ: Have you made a presentation at work?
answer: Yes, I made one last month for our project review.

en: He never comes late to meetings.
tamil: அவர் மீட்டிங்குக்கு ஒருநாளும் லேட்டா வர மாட்டாரு.
context: Praising a punctual colleague.
explain: 'Never' already makes the sentence negative, so do not add 'not'.
usage: Use it to talk about a colleague who is always on time.
leelaQ: Who is always on time in your office?
answer: My team lead is always on time for every meeting.

en: How long will the meeting take?
context: Asking the organiser about the time you need to keep free.
explain: 'How long' asks about the amount of time.
usage: Use it before a meeting when you need to plan your other work.
leelaQ: How long are your meetings usually?
answer: Most of them are thirty minutes to one hour.

en: Do you have five minutes to talk?
context: Asking a colleague for a short chat.
explain: Mentioning the time tells the person the talk will be short.
usage: Use it before you speak to a busy teammate so you do not disturb them.
leelaQ: How do you talk to a busy colleague?
answer: I ask politely if they have a few minutes first.

en: The deadline is next Wednesday.
context: Telling a teammate the last date for a task.
explain: A short and clear sentence with the simple present for a fixed date.
usage: Use it to remind a colleague of an important date.
leelaQ: When is your next deadline?
answer: My next deadline is the end of this month.

en: I will take notes during the meeting.
context: Volunteering to write the minutes.
explain: 'Will' is good when you offer to do something at that moment.
usage: Use it when the team needs someone to record the meeting points.
leelaQ: Do you like writing meeting notes?
answer: Yes, because I can remember all the points later.

en: We are meeting the client at ten tomorrow.
tamil: நாளைக்கு பத்து மணிக்கு கிளையன்ட்டை சந்திக்கப் போறோம்.
context: Sharing a fixed plan with a teammate.
explain: The present continuous with a time like 'tomorrow' shows a fixed plan.
usage: Use it when you tell your colleagues about an arranged appointment.
leelaQ: What are you doing tomorrow morning at work?
answer: I am attending a team meeting at ten o'clock.

en: Could you share the file with me?
context: Asking a teammate for a document.
explain: 'Could you' is a polite way to ask someone for something.
usage: Use it with a teammate or senior when you need a document.
leelaQ: How do you ask for a file from a colleague?
answer: I say could you share the file with me, please.

en: Could you remind me about the deadline tomorrow?
tamil: நாளைக்கு டெட்லைனைப் பத்தி எனக்கு நினைவூட்ட முடியுமா?
context: Asking a teammate to help you remember.
explain: 'Remind me about' asks someone to bring something to your mind.
usage: Use it with a teammate when you have many tasks and fear you may forget.
leelaQ: How do you remember your tasks?
answer: I write them in my notebook and set reminders on my phone.

en: Have you finished the testing?
context: Checking the work status with a teammate.
explain: 'Have you finished' asks about a result up to now.
usage: Use it as a team lead or a teammate who is waiting for a result.
leelaQ: What have you finished this week?
answer: I have finished two tasks and started a new one.

en: Why did they postpone the client meeting?
context: Asking a colleague about a sudden change.
explain: 'Postpone' means to move something to a later time.
usage: Use it when you hear a meeting is delayed and you want the reason.
leelaQ: What do you do when a meeting is postponed?
answer: I use the free time to finish my pending work.

en: I am not comfortable with this plan.
context: Raising a doubt about a plan honestly.
explain: 'Not comfortable' is a soft way to say you do not agree.
usage: Use it in a meeting when you have a doubt but do not want to sound rude.
leelaQ: How do you say you do not like a plan politely?
answer: I say I am not comfortable and I explain my reason.

en: Could you please extend the deadline by one day?
context: Asking a manager for more time.
explain: 'Extend' means to make longer. 'By one day' shows how much.
usage: Use it with a manager or client when you need a little more time.
leelaQ: Have you ever asked for an extension?
answer: Yes, I asked for one more day to check my work.

en: We are discussing the new schedule right now.
tamil: நாங்க இப்போ புது அட்டவணையைப் பத்தி பேசிட்டு இருக்கோம்.
context: Telling someone why the team is busy in a meeting.
explain: 'Are discussing' with 'right now' shows an action happening at this moment.
usage: Use it when someone asks you what the team is doing at the moment.
leelaQ: What is your team discussing these days?
answer: We are discussing the project plan for next month.

en: I need two more days to complete this.
tamil: இதை முடிக்க எனக்கு இன்னும் ரெண்டு நாள் வேணும்.
context: Asking a manager for more time.
explain: 'Need' says what is required. 'Two more days' means extra days.
usage: Use it with a manager when a task is taking longer than planned.
leelaQ: What do you say when you need more time?
answer: I explain my reason and tell them how many days I need.

en: Our team always shares updates on Monday mornings.
tamil: எங்க டீம் எப்பவும் திங்கள் காலைல அப்டேட் பகிர்ந்துக்கும்.
context: Describing your team's weekly habit to a new joiner.
explain: 'Always' with the simple present talks about a regular habit.
usage: Use it when you explain your team routine to a new colleague.
leelaQ: What does your team do on Monday mornings?
answer: We share our weekly updates and plan the tasks.

en: Let me explain my point once again.
context: Politely taking the floor in a discussion.
explain: 'Let me' asks permission and offers to do something.
usage: Use it in a meeting when people misunderstood what you said.
leelaQ: What do you do if people misunderstand you?
answer: I say it again in simple words and give an example.

en: My manager gave me good feedback today.
tamil: என் மேனேஜர் இன்னைக்கு எனக்கு நல்ல ஃபீட்பேக் கொடுத்தாரு.
context: Sharing happy news with a friend at work.
explain: 'Gave' is the past of 'give'. 'Feedback' is not used in the plural form.
usage: Use it with friends or family when you want to share a good day at work.
leelaQ: What feedback did your manager give you last time?
answer: He said my work is neat and I should speak more in meetings.

en: We are working on the final changes.
tamil: நாங்க இறுதி மாற்றங்கள்ல வேலை பண்ணிட்டு இருக்கோம்.
context: Updating a client on the work status.
explain: 'Are working on' shows that the task is still in progress.
usage: Use it when a client or manager asks for a status update.
leelaQ: What are you working on at the moment?
answer: I am working on a small report for my team.

en: Please give me your feedback by evening.
context: Asking a reviewer for a deadline.
explain: 'By evening' sets a limit of time politely.
usage: Use it when you need comments on your work before the end of the day.
leelaQ: When do you need feedback on your work?
answer: I need it before I send it to the client.

en: The client liked the first design.
context: Sharing good news about the client's reaction.
explain: 'Liked' is the past of 'like'. It is a simple way to report someone's reaction.
usage: Use it when you pass on the client's opinion to your team or manager.
leelaQ: How did your client react to your last work?
answer: The client liked it and asked for a few small changes.

en: Please send me the meeting link.
context: Asking a colleague for an online meeting link.
explain: 'Please' makes the order polite.
usage: Use it when you cannot find the link of an online meeting.
leelaQ: What do you ask when you cannot join an online call?
answer: I ask my colleague to send me the meeting link again.

en: Do you need any help from me?
tamil: உங்களுக்கு என்கிட்ட இருந்து ஏதாவது உதவி வேணுமா?
context: Offering support to a busy colleague.
explain: 'Do you need' is a kind way to offer help.
usage: Use it with a teammate who has a lot of work.
leelaQ: How do you offer help to a colleague?
answer: I ask if they need any help and then I take a small task.

en: I cannot attend the meeting today.
context: Informing the organiser that you will miss the meeting.
explain: 'Cannot' is the strong negative of 'can'. Add a reason to sound polite.
usage: Use it with a manager or organiser when you are not able to come.
leelaQ: What do you say when you cannot join a meeting?
answer: I say sorry and give my reason, and I ask for the notes.

en: Who is leading the project?
context: Asking a new colleague about project ownership.
explain: 'Who' as a subject is followed by 'is' and the verb with 'ing'.
usage: Use it when you join a new team and want to know who to talk to.
leelaQ: Who leads the project you work on?
answer: My senior colleague leads it, and I report to him.

en: Please let me know if anything changes.
context: Ending a message politely with a request.
explain: 'Let me know' is a very common and friendly phrase.
usage: Use it at the end of a message when plans are not final.
leelaQ: What do you say at the end of a work message?
answer: I say please let me know if you need anything.

en: I will not be able to meet the deadline.
context: Warning your manager early about a delay.
explain: 'Will not be able to' is a formal way to say you cannot do something later.
usage: Use it to tell your manager about a delay as early as you can.
leelaQ: What should you do if you cannot meet a deadline?
answer: I should tell my manager early and ask for more time.

en: The new joiner is learning very fast.
tamil: புதுசா சேர்ந்தவங்க ரொம்ப வேகமா கத்துக்கிட்டு இருக்காங்க.
context: Praising a new teammate to the manager.
explain: 'Is learning' shows a change that is happening now. 'Joiner' is common in Indian offices.
usage: Use it to give a good report about a new team member.
leelaQ: Who helped you when you joined your office?
answer: My senior colleague helped me and showed me everything.

en: Sorry, I was not in the office yesterday.
context: Explaining why you missed something.
explain: 'Was not' is the past negative of 'is'. Start with 'sorry' to be polite.
usage: Use it when someone asks about a task you could not see because you were away.
leelaQ: Why do people take leave from the office?
answer: They take leave for health, family work or a short trip.
